newsitem.title: USA: Baker Hughes to acquire Petrolite in $693 million deal.
newsitem.headline: Baker Hughes to acquire Petrolite in $693 million deal.

text.p: Petrolite Corp., a speciality chemicals maker, said Wednesday it has agreed to be acquired by Baker Hughes Inc. in a stock swap worth about $693 million.

The deal includes Baker Hughes' acquisition of Wm. S. Barnickel & Co., a closely held company that is Petrolite's largest shareholder, the companies said. Barnickel, which has a 47 percent stake in Petrolite, holds the shares of the founders and early employees of Petrolite and is seen as the impetus behind the sale.
Baker Hughes, a Houston-based company that sells oil and gas products and services, will offer $61 worth of its common stock for each of Petrolite's 11.36 million shares in a tax-free exchange.
The exact exchange ratio will be based on the average market price of Baker Hughes stock over 10 days prior to closing, Petrolite said. Analysts said the deal was expected to close in July or August.
Petrolite stock soared $10.375 on the Nasdaq to $58.375 in response to the deal, analysts said. Baker Hughes was unchanged at $35.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.

"It makes a lot of strategic sense," said Geoffrey Kieburtz, an analyst for investment bankers Salomon Brothers. "Because of the competition for the business, they had to pay quite a full price, but based on what the company indicated it will be accretive to 1998 earnings."
Petrolite, a more than 80-year old company, earlier this month put off its March 3 annual meeting, citing a possible sale or merger of the company.
In November, Petrolite said it had formed a special committee to explore sale or merger options and that it had rejected earlier offers of $44 per share or less as "clearly indaequate."
Although quite a jump from previous offers, analysts said the $61 a share deal is within expectations.
"Their best (earnings) numbers are in front of them over the next three to four years," Russell Hoffman, an analyst for investment bankers Bear, Stearns & Co., said of Petrolite.
For its fiscal year ended Oct. 31, St. Louis-based Petrolite had sales of $361 million, down from $364.8 million a year ago.

Petrolite's special committee was initially formed because of concerns Barnickel was considering a sale or merger of Petrolite and would go through with it without "regard to whether maximum shareholder value can be realised".
Paul Hatfield, chairman of Petrolite, said in a statement that the deal "will expand Petrolite's ability to create value for our shareholders, customers, business partners and employees".
The agreement with Baker Hughes is subject to approval by shareholders of Petrolite and Barnickel, Petrolite said, as well as other customary conditions.
John Casper, Petrolite's chief financial officer, said in an interview that shareholders' response to the deal has been "generally favourable".
Analysts said Baker Hughes indicated that the acquisition would save the company about $25 million annually in its performance chemicals business, a number analysts said could prove to be larger.

"Combining the operations and people of Petrolite with Baker Performance Chemicals will allow Baker Hughes to bring unprecedented technology and service levels to its customers around the world," Max Lukens, chairman of Baker Hughes, said in a statement.
Petrolite and Baker Hughes are currently competitors in performance chemicals, which play a role in improving production rates in oil fields.
